w: Capital of the Berber kingdom of Numidia, allied with Rome through the Punic Wars before Julius Caesar folded it into Roman rule. Destroyed early in the 4th century, it was rebuilt by Emperor Constantine, who renamed it after himself. Punic inscriptions called the Cirta steles survive from the site.
_facts: Capital of the Berber kingdom of Numidia
Allied with Rome during the Punic Wars, 264-146 BC
Rebuilt by Emperor Constantine after destruction, who renamed it after himself
Site of the Cirta steles, a corpus of Punic inscriptions

w: Named for Emir Abdelkader, this Sunni mosque ranks as the second-largest in Algeria, surpassed only by the Djamaa El Djazair in Algiers. Its scale makes it one of Constantine's most prominent modern landmarks, a counterweight in a city already dense with older mosques, Ottoman palaces and famous gorge bridges.
_facts: Named for Emir Abdelkader
Second-largest mosque in Algeria after the Djamaa El Djazair in Algiers
Recognised as an architectural landmark

w: A 164-metre suspension bridge across the Rhumel gorge, opened to traffic in April 1912. Until 1929 it was the highest bridge in the world, its deck sitting 175 metres above the river. Designed by French engineer Ferdinand Arnodin, it links the Casbah to Sidi M'Cid hill; cables were replaced in a 2000 restoration.
_facts: 164 metres long, opened April 1912
Highest bridge in the world until 1929, at 175m above the river
Designed by Ferdinand Arnodin
Links the Casbah to Sidi M'Cid hill

w: The oldest of Constantine's famous gorge bridges, rebuilt several times: an Ottoman multi-arch bridge in 1792, a French iron arch in 1863, and today's concrete arch. A natural rock formation spans the gorge almost directly beneath it, hiding much of the river, with remains of earlier stone bridges visible on top.
_facts: Oldest of Constantine's eight famous bridges
Rebuilt as Ottoman arch (1792), French iron arch (1863), then concrete arch
A natural rock 'bridge' sits almost directly beneath it
Remains of earlier stone bridges are visible atop the natural span

w: Built between 1908 and 1912 by engineer Aubin Eyraud, with Paul Sejourne designing the hangers, this 447-metre viaduct crosses the Rhumel gorge on 27 arches, the tallest reaching 107 metres. It was the tallest concrete bridge in the world when built, linking the Coudiat city centre to the train station.
_facts: Built 1908-1912 by Aubin Eyraud with Paul Sejourne
447 metres long, 27 arches, tallest reaching 107 metres
Was the tallest concrete bridge in the world when built
Links Coudiat district to Constantine train station

w: Constantine's Ottoman-era Bey's Palace was among the city's main showcase sites when Constantine was named Arab Capital of Culture in 2015. It stands today as one of the city's principal historic buildings surviving from the period of Ottoman rule, a counterpart to Oran's own Bey's Palace from the same era.
_facts: Historic Ottoman-era palace in Constantine
Also known as Ahmad Bey Palace
Featured among the main sights during Constantine's 2015 Arab Capital of Culture selection

w: A cable-stayed bridge spanning the Rhumel gorge, 1,119 metres long, named for Salah Bey, whose 1771-1792 rule brought major urban works to Constantine. With its futuristic, modern design, it is already counted as an eighth wonder alongside the city's seven historic bridges.
_facts: 1,119 metres long, cable-stayed
Named for Salah Bey, who ruled Constantine 1771-1792
Called an 'eighth wonder' alongside the city's seven historic bridges

w: Founded as the Souk El Ghezel Mosque, also called the Ghazal Market Mosque, and completed in 1730. From 1838 until 1962 the French repurposed the building as the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows, before it was restored as a mosque after independence, having swapped faiths twice in under two centuries.
s: Mosque, then cathedral, then mosque again
_facts: Completed as a mosque in 1730, originally the Souk El Ghezel Mosque
Repurposed as a Catholic cathedral from 1838 to 1962
Restored to use as a mosque in 1962
Officially the Hussein Bey Mosque, also known as El Bey Mosque

w: A 125-metre suspension footbridge across the Rhumel, opened in April 1925, once the third-highest bridge in the world at 110 metres. Designed by Ferdinand Arnodin, it links Larbi Ben M'hidi Street to Romania Road, joining the train station district to the old town by a staircase or the Merdersa lift.
_facts: 125 metres long, opened April 1925
Once the world's third-highest bridge, at 110m
Designed by Ferdinand Arnodin
Links the train station district to the old town via a staircase or the Merdersa lift

w: A white colonial-era hotel on the edge of Place des Martyrs, at 1 Avenue Rahmani Achour, its name recalling ancient Cirta, the Roman-era city that stood on this ground before Constantine. It remains the property of the Societe de l'Hotel Cirta, owned by Algerian businessman and philanthropist Mohand Tiar.
s: Colonial hotel named for ancient Cirta
_facts: White colonial building at 1 Avenue Rahmani Achour
On the edge of Place des Martyrs
Owned by the Societe de l'Hotel Cirta, whose owner is Mohand Tiar
